<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The comment's empirical sections are mostly sound and useful. Its conclusion is not. The documented corrections cut the Halden per-hour gain from 23.4% to 10.8%, but they do not take it to zero. The step from "about 11% remains" to "entirely an artifact" rests on an untested novelty argument. That argument ignores the strongest contrary evidence, which is a randomised trial the authors cite elsewhere. The comment also contains internal inconsistencies, and it mischaracterises the Varden meetings analysis.

## Arithmetic checks

| Claim | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Actual hours, 27 orgs | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Actual hours, 17 orgs | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Table 2 row 2 | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Table 2 row 3 | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Table 2 row 4 | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |
| Hours overstatement | 20.0 − 14.1 | 5.9 points ✓ |

Two figures do not reconcile.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Start from 32 scheduled hours. Adding 0.7 extra hours on each of four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours on the day off (1.6 hours) gives about 36.4 hours, not 34.6. Starting instead from baseline daily hours (40.3 / 5 = 8.06) gives about 36.6. Either the two "sources" are measured on different bases, such as averages over different groups of staff, or the 34.6 figure is wrong. If the components are right, actual hours fell by only about 10%, and the authors have *understated* their own point. This needs reconciling either way.

**The novelty extrapolation is off.** Energy was +0.61 SD at month three and +0.29 SD at month six. A straight line through those two points reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor in itself. The larger problem is extrapolating linearly from two points at all (see below).

## What the comment does well

- **Attrition.** If the microdata show that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule started, and that six of the nine cited workload or output, that is a serious misstatement in the working paper. It is the comment's most important finding. The working paper's authors should respond.
- **Record-based output.** Comparing the manager index with record-based indices in the 23 organisations that submitted records is exactly the right check. A gap in 19 of 23 organisations is unlikely to be chance; a sign test gives p ≈ 0.001.
- **Actual hours.** Using time-tracking logs to replace scheduled hours is a proper fix. The result (≈ −14% rather than −20%) is very close to Varden's timesheet figure for case-processing (−13%).
- **Revenue and sectors.** The inflation adjustment and the point that any index above 80 shows a per-hour "gain" are correct. I raised both points in my review of the working paper.
- **The data note is candid.** It says the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets.

## Main problems

**1. The conclusion is not supported by the comment's own evidence.**
After correction, a gain of about 11% in output per actual hour remains. The claim that this residual is "entirely an artifact" depends on the novelty argument in §6, which is not tested (problem 4). The claim also extends to "reduced-hours schemes" in general, while the data note correctly says the estimates describe only subsets of one pilot. The note and the conclusion contradict each other.

**2. The abstract misdescribes Table 2.**
The abstract says that correcting "the first three" problems (attrition, output measure, hours) gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only the output measure and hours. Attrition is not corrected anywhere, and no bound is computed for it. The abstract also says four problems "account for most of the reported gain," but the revenue comparison has no bearing on output per hour.

A simple intention-to-treat bound would help. For example, recompute the 70-organisation mean under assumed output for the nine withdrawals, such as an index of 80, meaning no per-hour gain. That would make the attrition point quantitative instead of rhetorical.

**3. Table 2 compares different samples.**
The four rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The step-by-step drop therefore mixes the effect of each correction with changes in which organisations are included. All four specifications should be reported on the common subset of 17 organisations. That means the manager index with scheduled hours, the record index with scheduled hours, the manager index with actual hours, and the record index with actual hours.

**4. The novelty argument is untested, although the data to test it exist.**
- Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the comment's authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline over months three to six. They do not show this trajectory.
- Self-reported energy is not output. A fall in energy is not evidence of a fall in productivity.
- Drawing a straight line through two survey points to find a "return to baseline" is not a basis for inference.
- "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is reasonable as a reason to withhold judgement. It does not justify asserting the opposite. "Entirely an artifact" is itself a positive claim and needs evidence.

**5. The Varden trial is cited selectively.**
The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention Varden's case-processing result. That result is +12.5% in output per *actual* hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4), measured from administrative records, against a randomised control, at nine months, with no attrition problem. It addresses exactly the selection, measurement and hours problems the comment raises. It is also longer than the period over which the comment says novelty fades. It is also similar in size to the comment's own corrected 10.8%. A comment arguing that per-hour gains are entirely artifactual has to engage with this result.

**6. The meetings section misrepresents the Varden analysis.**
- The seven offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known." They are all of the treated case-processing offices, a stratum fixed before randomisation.
- The meetings data were collected at month six, before the nine-month results existed.
- Varden also reports a treated-versus-control difference in meeting time (3.8 v 7.1 hours a week). That is a comparison between randomised groups, not only the seven-office correlation.
- The Varden authors already state every caveat the comment raises, and they registered a confirmatory test.
- The comment holds a different standard for its own §6, which is also post hoc, unregistered, and based on two survey time points.

There is also a conceptual problem. If meeting cuts explain the gain, the gain is a *real* reorganisation effect: low-value time was removed. It may not be caused by rest, and it might be achievable without cutting hours. But it is not an "artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." The comment treats "not caused by fatigue reduction" as if it meant "not real."

## Secondary points

- **Billable hours are a biased output measure here.** Some record-based indices use "billable hours delivered," which falls mechanically when hours are cut. For professional-services firms, the record-based index is therefore biased *downward* as a measure of output. The comment should say how many of the 23 used this measure, and show results excluding them.
- **Weighting is not stated.** It is unclear whether Tables 1 and 2 are weighted by employees, as in the working paper, or by organisation.
- **CPI is a rough deflator for revenue.** Sector-specific price indices, or comparison with non-participating firms' revenue growth, would be better. The direction of the correction is still right.
- **The retail finding rests on three organisations.** The −11.2% record-based fall comes from only three organisations. It is consistent with Varden but is thin evidence on its own.
- **Logged hours may be incomplete.** Time-tracking may miss work, as the authors note, so actual hours probably fell by even less than 14%. This would reduce the corrected gain further, which favours the comment's direction.

## Where the evidence stands across the three documents

| | Gain in output per hour | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Halden as reported | +23.4% | Manager index, scheduled hours, survivors |
| Halden corrected (17 orgs) | +10.8% | Record-based output, actual hours, survivors, non-random subset |
| Varden, case-processing | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | Randomised, records, timesheets |
| Varden, counter/contact | +6.7% per hour, but −11.4% per employee | Randomised; per-hour gain likely reflects higher utilisation |

A defensible reading:

- The headline 23% figure was inflated by roughly half.
- In work where output isn't tied to presence, a per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% appears to survive the corrections and randomisation, at least to nine months.
- Its mechanism (rest, meeting cuts, or novelty) and its durability remain open questions.
- Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output and service.

The comment establishes the first point well and supports the last. It does not establish that the remaining gain is zero.

Its recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, follow-up of 18 months or more, and analysis of all enrolled organisations. They largely describe what Varden already did.

I can draft a referee report, or a short reply letter from either the Halden or the Varden authors' perspective.
